Spikenard
SPIKE-nard
n.
Latin spica nardi, “spike of nard”; a costly aromatic ointment derived from the spikenard plant (Nardostachys jatamansi) native to the Himalayas, expensive to import to Palestine, used in luxury anointings.

📖 Biblical Definition

Spikenard is the costly aromatic ointment derived from the spikenard plant (Nardostachys jatamansi) native to the Himalayas, imported at great expense to the ancient Mediterranean world and used in luxury anointings. The substance is referenced twice in the Song of Solomon as part of the bride’s and the bridegroom’s mutual delights: while the king sitteth at his table, my spikenard sendeth forth the smell thereof (Song 1:12); spikenard and saffron; calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense; myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices (Song 4:14). But its supreme biblical appearance is in the anointing-of-Christ narratives of Mark 14:3-9 and John 12:1-8. Mary of Bethany breaks an alabaster box of spikenard very precious and pours it on Christ’s head (Mark) or anoints His feet and wipes them with her hair (John); the disciples—and notably Judas, who would shortly betray Him for thirty pieces of silver—object that this ointment might have been sold for more than three hundred pence (denarii), and given to the poor. Christ’s response is one of the most theologically dense passages in the Gospels: let her alone; against the day of my burying hath she kept this. For the poor always ye have with you; but me ye have not always... Verily I say unto you, Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached throughout the whole world, this also that she hath done shall be spoken of for a memorial of her. Several structural points emerge from the narrative. First, the cost: three hundred denarii is approximately a year’s wages for a laborer; Mary’s gift is genuinely costly, not symbolic-poverty. Second, the timing: Mary alone among Christ’s associates grasps that He is about to die, and her anointing is, in His own words, against the day of my burying—a prophetic act of preparation that the male disciples, who had heard Christ predict His death repeatedly, had not understood. Third, the criticism: Judas’s objection (with the cover of concern for the poor masking his own thievery, John 12:6) is the precise type of pious-sounding rationalization that has always been deployed against costly devotion to Christ. Fourth, Christ’s vindication: Mary’s extravagance, criticized in its moment, is canonized in the Gospels as the perpetual memorial of devotion wheresoever this gospel shall be preached throughout the whole world—and the Gospel narrators have preserved the memorial as Christ commanded. The spikenard-narrative therefore stands as Scripture’s great teaching on costly devotion to Christ: real cost, prophetic insight, vindicated by Christ over the criticism of the merely-practical, canonized for the encouragement of every subsequent saint who has been criticized for similarly extravagant devotion to the Lord who deserves it.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SPIKENARD as a plant of the genus Nardostachys, and the costly aromatic ointment derived from it; in scripture, the precious ointment Mary of Bethany poured on Christ in anticipation of His burial (John 12:3), commended by Christ over the criticism of His disciples and canonized as the perpetual memorial of costly devotion.

SPIKENARD, n. — 1. A plant of the genus Nardostachys, growing in the mountains of India. 2. An aromatic essential oil obtained from this plant, used as a perfume and as a costly anointing oil. Mary took a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly (John 12:3).

NARD, n. — (See SPIKENARD.) An aromatic plant and the costly ointment derived from it.

📖 Key Scripture

John 12:3 — "Then took Mary a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly, and anointed the feet of Jesus, and wiped his feet with her hair: and the house was filled with the odour of the ointment."

Mark 14:3 — "And being in Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he sat at meat, there came a woman having an alabaster box of ointment of spikenard very precious; and she brake the box, and poured it on his head."

Mark 14:9 — "Verily I say unto you, Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached throughout the whole world, this also that she hath done shall be spoken of for a memorial of her."

Song of Solomon 1:12 — "While the king sitteth at his table, my spikenard sendeth forth the smell thereof."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The spikenard-narrative is corrupted, in contemporary application, by the Judas-style rationalization that mistakes mere practicality for biblical wisdom and criticizes costly devotion to Christ as wasteful—and by the inverse sentimentalization that has lost the prophetic and costly substance of Mary’s act and treats it as a feel-good story without the structural challenge to comfortable Christianity.

expand to see more

The Judas-style rationalization is the precise pattern Christ rebuked at the dinner in Bethany, and the pattern recurs in every age. Costly devotion to Christ—the disproportionate giving to gospel-mission, the sacrificial generosity that puts the kingdom first, the extravagant offering that the merely-practical would call wasteful—is met with the pious-sounding objection: this might have been better used elsewhere; the cost is excessive; surely something more modest would have served as well. Judas’s motive in John 12 is exposed as theft hidden behind concern for the poor; the modern Judas-style criticism may have purer motives, but it deploys the same logic against the same kind of devotion. Christ’s response in the narrative is the standing answer: let her alone... the poor always ye have with you; but me ye have not always. Devotion to Christ has its own logic, and the criticism of the merely-practical is to be answered in His name. The recovery is the freedom to give extravagantly to Christ where the heart is moved to do so, with the assurance that what looks wasteful to the practical is canonized by Christ as memorial-worthy.

The opposite contemporary corruption is the sentimentalization that has lost the prophetic and costly substance of Mary’s act and treats it as a feel-good story without the structural challenge to comfortable Christianity. Mary’s gift cost a year’s wages; she grasped Christ’s imminent death when the male disciples did not; her act was prophetic insight expressed in extravagant devotion. The sentimentalized version that turns Mary into a generic figure of doing a sweet thing for Jesus misses the specific costliness, the specific prophetic insight, and the specific challenge the narrative poses to those who would never give a year’s wages to anything that did not have an obvious return-on-investment. Recover both ends. Refuse the Judas-style rationalization that criticizes costly devotion as wasteful, and refuse the sentimentalization that strips the narrative of its prophetic and costly substance. The biblical spikenard-narrative is Christ’s perpetual encouragement to every saint who, like Mary, is moved to costly devotion to Him, against the criticism of those who do not understand what only the Spirit teaches the loving heart to grasp.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin spica nardi (spike of nard); the costly aromatic ointment from the Himalayan spikenard plant; supreme biblical use is Mary of Bethany’s anointing of Christ’s feet/head in anticipation of His burial (John 12:3; Mark 14:3), commended by Christ over the disciples’ objections and canonized as the perpetual memorial of costly devotion.

expand to see more

Greek nardos pistikē (G3487 + G4101) — pure nard, genuine spikenard (Mark 14:3; John 12:3).

Hebrew nērd (H5373) — spikenard (Song 1:12; 4:13-14).

Latin spica nardi — spike of nard (the source of English spikenard).

Greek muron (G3464) — ointment (the general term; spikenard was a specific costly variety).

Usage

"Mary of Bethany’s spikenard (a year’s wages of ointment) was poured on Christ in prophetic anticipation of His burial."

"Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached throughout the whole world, this also that she hath done shall be spoken of for a memorial of her—Christ canonized the act in His own commission to the Gospel-writers."

"Judas-style rationalization criticizes costly devotion as wasteful; sentimentalization loses the prophetic and costly substance; biblical spikenard-narrative is Christ’s standing vindication of extravagant devotion against the merely-practical."
